revised_comments: The ITU Digital Development Dashboard reports Libya's mobile broadband basket (data-only plan) at 3.6% of GNI per capita in 2021, within the moderate affordability band (2-5% of GNI per capita) and above the UN Broadband Commission's 2% target. Related baskets show wider variation: the low-consumption mobile data and voice basket stands at 2.3% and the high-consumption basket at 6.2% of GNI per capita.

IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. The Central Bank of Libya's Data Protection System and Executive Regulation (Circular No. 18, dated 1 June 2025) explicitly prohibits storing personal, financial, credit or sensitive data outside Libya for all CBL-supervised entities (banks, foreign bank branches, fintechs, payment/exchange/leasing companies); it becomes mandatory from 1 July 2026, with fines of LYD 100,000 per violation. Separately, Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions (Article 78) imposes conditions on cross-border transfer of personal data by authentication service providers. Score revised from 0 to 3 (sectoral requirements only, financial sector), since the requirement does not yet extend beyond the financial sector.
revised_comments: Libya has a sectoral data localisation requirement: the Central Bank of Libya's Data Protection System and Executive Regulation (Circular No. 18, June 2025) prohibits banks, fintechs, payment providers and other CBL-supervised entities from storing personal, financial, credit or sensitive data outside Libya, with fines of LYD 100,000 per violation; the requirement becomes mandatory from 1 July 2026. The 2022 Electronic Transactions Law separately places conditions on cross-border transfers of personal data by authentication service providers, but there is no economy-wide data localisation law.

Comments: No data found; cloud adoption studies ongoing

revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited (comment noted 'cloud adoption studies ongoing'). Libya's General Information Authority (GIA) published a National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation, approved by the Prime Minister in April 2025, which calls explicitly for establishing a national government data centre as the nucleus of a government cloud and a national disaster-recovery centre. As of January 2026, GIA presented a proposed National Cloud Computing Policy (with ESCWA), still at proposal stage, and a February 2026 workshop discussed data-centre service roadmaps under the National Strategy for Communications and Informatics (2023-2027); no operational national data centre or adopted cloud strategy is yet confirmed. Score revised from 0 to 2 (planned/under construction).
revised_comments: Libya's General Information Authority has approved (April 2025) a National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation that calls for establishing a national government data centre as the nucleus of a government cloud, alongside a national disaster-recovery centre. As of early 2026, a National Cloud Computing Policy has been proposed (in partnership with ESCWA) and roadmaps for data-centre services are under active discussion through the National Strategy for Communications and Informatics (2023-2027), but no national government data centre or adopted cloud strategy is yet operational.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. World Bank/ESMAP SDG7 tracking data show electricity access at 100.0% for urban Libya (2023) versus only 0.8% for rural Libya, but the rural figure has not been updated since 2012 (an 11-year gap between the two data points), and 0.8% appears anomalously low relative to Libya's high overall electrification rate and pre-2011 rural figures near 99%. This mismatch likely reflects data collection breakdown following the 2011 conflict rather than a genuine, current gap of this magnitude. Tentatively coded 1 (gap >60pp) on the raw figures, but flagged for human review given the stale and possibly anomalous rural data point.
revised_comments: World Bank/ESMAP data show near-universal electricity access in urban Libya (100% as of 2023) contrasted with a much lower rural figure of 0.8%, though this rural estimate dates to 2012 and pre-dates more recent improvements, so the current gap is likely narrower than the raw figures suggest.
